  trauma_type: Trauma to a loved one
  pcl5: 58

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Moral Violation: People misbehaving, Funerals/Graves: Funerals, cemeteries, or grief-related events, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell
  Threat: Body Reacts Before Mind: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think, False Alarms: I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
  Memory: No Coherent Story: I cannot tell a clear story of what happened even to myself, Guilt on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt, Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Happiness: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable., Life Destroyed: My life has been destroyed by the trauma, Lost Meaning: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore

Vignette:
Kaikea had always been close to his younger sister, Leilani. Growing up in a tight-knit Samoan community in Southern California, they shared everything from childhood secrets to adult struggles. So when Leilani was killed in a drunk-driving accident on her 21st birthday, Kaikea's world was shattered. The driver, a friend of Leilani's, had been behind the wheel after a night of partying, and Kaikea couldn't shake the feeling that he should have been there to stop it. In the months following the funeral, Kaikea found himself increasingly on edge. He would catch whiffs of beer or liquor and feel his heart racing, as if he was back at the hospital waiting for news about Leilani's condition. Even walking past cemeteries or seeing hearses on the road would send him into a panic, his mind flooded with images of Leilani's coffin being lowered into the ground. He began to avoid social gatherings where alcohol might be present, turning down invitations from friends and family. As a pharmacist, Kaikea was used to being composed under pressure, but lately, he'd been jumping at every little noise in the store. His coworkers commented on his increased irritability, and customers started to notice that he seemed distracted, as if his mind was elsewhere. Kaikea knew it wasn't just grief; his body felt like it was constantly bracing for impact, waiting for the next blow. When people asked him about Leilani's death, Kaikea struggled to piece together a coherent story. He'd try to explain what happened, but the words would get jumbled, and he'd end up feeling overwhelmed by guilt. Why hadn't he been there to protect her? Why had he let her go out that night? The questions swirled in his head like a toxic mix of emotions. Sometimes, when memories of Leilani surfaced, Kaikea felt numb, as if he was observing the events from outside his body. Other times, the pain was so intense it left him breathless. He'd see Leilani's smile or hear her laughter and be hit with a wave of grief that would leave him shaking. Kaikea had always been a happy person, but now he felt like he was just going through the motions. Nothing brought him joy; everything reminded him of what he'd lost. His relationships suffered as he withdrew from friends and family, unable to bear their questions or their attempts at comfort. Even his work, once a source of pride, now felt empty and meaningless. One day, while restocking shelves, Kaikea's manager approached him about his performance. Customers had been complaining about his short temper, and the store was starting to suffer. Kaikea knew he needed help; he couldn't keep living like this. The thought of facing another year without Leilani, trapped in this cycle of guilt and anxiety, was too much to bear. With a sense of desperation, he made an appointment with a therapist, hoping to find a way out of the darkness that had consumed him. As Kaikea sat in his small apartment, staring blankly at the wall, he couldn't shake the feeling that his life was destroyed, that nothing would ever be the same again. What scared him most was the thought of losing himself completely, of becoming a shadow of the person he once was. He knew it wouldn't bring Leilani back, but maybe, just maybe, therapy could help him find a way to live with the pain, to rediscover some sense of purpose and meaning in a world that now felt empty and cruel.
